evidence.title: Risk Factors for Nondiagnostic Imaging in a Real-World Deployment of Artificial Intelligence Diabetic Retinal Examinations in an Integrated Healthcare System: Maximizing Workflow Efficiency Through Predictive Dilation
evidence.venue: Journal of diabetes science and technology
evidence.outcome: Rate of nondiagnostic (ungradable) results in real-world autonomous AI retinal exams
evidence.effect: Of 241 patients, 123 (51%) had nondiagnostic results; T1D (aOR 5.82), smoking (aOR 2.86), and age per 10 years (aOR 2.12) were associated with nondiagnostic results.
evidence.quote: Of 241 patients (59% female; median age = 59), 123 (51%) had nondiagnostic results.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether an unavailable indication or labeling about missing inputs changes clinician reliance on degraded AI outputs. Two deployment studies show that absent or nondiagnostic results occur often enough to matter, and the support for this recommendation rests on FDA draft guidance and the CHAI framework.

perspectives.view: No included study compares tools that display an unavailable indication with tools that do not, and none evaluates labeling about missing inputs. The two level 3 studies document how often results are missing. They cannot show that the display or the labeling reduces harm, so certainty about the practice's effect cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In a stroke triage deployment, 79 of 704 cases at one hospital and 20 of 642 at another had no CADt result. If a missing result is silent or looks like a negative, clinicians may deprioritize a large vessel occlusion. An explicit unavailable flag targets this failure mode, but the studies do not test whether it catches errors.

The rate of missing output differed between two hospitals running the same stroke tool, and an autonomous retinal exam returned nondiagnostic results for 123 of 241 patients (51%). These figures suggest that missing-result handling is a routine workflow event. How an unavailable flag is displayed and acted on remains unstudied.

In the retinal study, type 1 diabetes (aOR 5.82), smoking (aOR 2.86), and age per 10 years (aOR 2.12) were associated with nondiagnostic results. This suggests that missing outputs may concentrate in identifiable patient groups, so labeling that describes which inputs or patients yield unavailable results may matter for fair use.

FDA draft guidance recommends that marketing submissions explain how lost inputs may affect performance when they can prevent an output. The CHAI guide describes an unavailable error indication as a design element. Neither source is binding, and the FDA document remains in draft form.

A 51% nondiagnostic rate in an autonomous retinal program means that about half of screened patients may need a repeat or referral pathway. Systems that deploy such tools may need staffing and scheduling for unavailable results, whether or not the tool flags them clearly.

When half of retinal exams are nondiagnostic, patients may leave without a usable result unless someone tells them and arranges follow-up. A visible unavailable indication may prompt that human contact, though no study has measured whether it does.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare clinician behavior and patient outcomes when AI tools show an explicit unavailable indication versus a silent or ambiguous missing result, and that test whether labeling about missing inputs changes how clinicians interpret or act on outputs.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and neither hazard study reports enrollment of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of unavailable indications and missing-input labeling in these groups is unknown, although the retinal study suggests that nondiagnostic rates vary by patient characteristics.
